A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoRA computational-complexity research. Their text, equations, and Appendices A–E are readable and support comparison; the shorter v2 retains the principal proofs while reorganizing the document.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical results and proofs, including in its appendices. References to empirical performance concern prior work; no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

after.justification: Section 6 reports the authors' speech fine-tuning experiments on LibriLight. Table 1 and Figure 1 present measured training times for standard and outlier-free OPT models at three sizes.

M1.justification: The LoRA objectives, partial/full attention-weight adaptation, tensor decomposition, and chained low-rank gradient approximations remain unchanged. Section 6 evaluates a previously published outlier-free architecture without introducing a new component into the paper's approximation construction.

E1.justification: v2 introduces actual dataset and task coverage where v1 had only theoretical settings: LibriLight speech data and cross-modality fine-tuning of OPT language models into speech/text models. This adds an empirical application domain, not merely another presentation of the generic attention problem.

E2.justification: v2 introduces the first evaluated comparison: LoRA on standard transformers versus LoRA on the outlier-free transformers of Hu et al. (2024a), reported separately for three OPT sizes in Table 1. v1 cites related architectures but does not evaluate them.

E3.justification: Section 6 adds a new experimental protocol using OPT-125M, OPT-350M, and OPT-1.3B, full LoRA adaptation of WK/WQ/WV, rank 128, alpha 256, and training time per epoch as the outcome. These are newly introduced experiments, not revisions to previously reported empirical settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds a focused case study asking whether outlier removal improves LoRA training efficiency and whether the gain varies with model size. Table 1 supplies this evidence, absent in v1, but there is no broader norm-threshold sweep, gradient-error analysis, or robustness study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The new timings in v2 are point values, and Figure 1 has no error bars.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first measured results: standard/outlier-free epoch times of 58/55 minutes for OPT-125M, 69/61 for OPT-350M, and 84/63 for OPT-1.3B. Table 1's time reductions are 5.2%, 11.6%, and 25.0%; the prose's 5.5%, 13.1%, and 33.3% speed increases use inverse-time ratios. These newly reported results show larger relative gains for larger models.

T1.justification: v2 corrects A's dimensions from r×b to r×a in Definition 1.1 and replaces Q-only derivative references with μ-indexed derivatives in Problem 1. The principal complexity bounds, assumptions, SETH reduction, and proofs in Appendices B–E are retained. The new informal Theorems 1.1–1.2 summarize existing results.

C1.justification: The two central contributions—norm-dependent computational hardness and existence of almost-linear approximation algorithms—remain intact. v2 additionally advertises practical implementation guidance and numerical justification, and explicitly asserts applicability without data/model assumptions beyond numerical encoding, expanding its stated practical scope.

C2.justification: v1 already links outliers to inefficiency in Appendix A. v2 develops this into specific recommendations for pre-activation normalization and outlier-removing activations in Remark 7.2, and interprets the new timings as support. Its limitations paragraph also replaces the generic lack-of-implementation caveat with a necessary-versus-sufficient-conditions qualification.

D1.justification: v2 adds concrete experimental documentation: LoRA rank and alpha, four NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80GB memory, PyTorch/Hugging Face software, and references for model training and speech adaptation. A first-page footnote states that code is available on OpenReview. This substantially expands practical reproducibility information, although batch size, learning rate, sequence length, and precise data selection remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Alman and Yu (2024), Pan et al. (2024), and works supporting normalization, OPT, LibriLight, and SpeechLM experiments. Remarks 1.1 and 7.2 make additional connections to sampling, quantization, and normalization methods. The existing novelty positioning as a computational-limits analysis of LoRA is retained.

P1.justification: v2 adds informal theorem summaries and explanations around the tensor definitions, supplies descriptive definition titles, and standardizes 'almost linear' terminology. It moves the SETH introduction to Section 5 and references before the appendices, and updates the title and author information. Most existing exposition and proof text remain closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 comprehensively retypesets the paper in ICLR format, changing typography, spacing, headers, mathematical styling, and equation layout. It combines the introduction with the title page and removes the separate full contents page. Table 1 and its accompanying bar chart, Figure 1, are new displays absent from v1.

improvement.justification: Clearer explanations, informal theorem summaries, small formal corrections, and the new OPT/LibriLight timing illustration provide a modest improvement over v1. The empirical support remains limited: it does not test almost-linear sequence-length scaling, gradient approximation accuracy, or preserved task quality, and reports no uncertainty. Section 7 also labels the upper-bound theorems' conditions as necessary although those theorems establish existence under those conditions, reducing the precision of the expanded practical interpretation.
